opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the really interesting things that's happened over the last few years is that synthetic data has become a kind of interface for telling models what we want from them. Traditionally, if you had some structural knowledge about a problem, say you knew the task was compositional, or you knew certain symmetries should hold, the way you'd get that into a model was by building it into the architecture. You'd design a special module, or a particular kind of inductive bias, and hope that it carried over to the data you actually cared about.

What we've found, and a lot of other people have found too, is that you can often get much of the same effect by expressing the constraint in the data instead of the model. Some of our earlier work on compositional data augmentation is a good example. If you believe that certain fragments of examples should be interchangeable, so that if "jump twice" and "walk twice" behave in parallel ways, then other contexts with "jump" should work like the same contexts with "walk," you can just write down that principle as a procedure for generating new training examples. Then a fairly generic sequence model trained on the augmented data ends up behaving much more like it has the inductive bias you wanted, without you having to hard-wire it.

I find that appealing for a couple of reasons. One is just practical: it's much easier to write a little program that generates data than to redesign an architecture and make sure it still scales and trains well. The other is more conceptual. It separates the question of what we believe about the world from the question of how we parameterize the learner. You can state your prior knowledge declaratively, as a distribution over examples, and let the learning algorithm figure out how to internalize it.

That said, there are real limits. Synthetic data only imposes a constraint as well as the generator captures it, and models are very good at picking up on artifacts of the generation process rather than the principle you intended. So you can end up teaching the model something about your sampler instead of something about the world. And for a lot of the properties we really care about now, things like truthfulness or consistency of beliefs across contexts, it's not obvious how to write down a generator at all. Increasingly the interesting move is having models themselves produce the synthetic data, checking it for consistency, and training on the cleaned-up version. That gets you a kind of self-improvement loop where the top-down constraint is something like "your answers should hang together coherently," which is much more abstract than the old symbolic augmentation rules, but it's the same basic idea.

r001.rationale: The response says constraints expressed in generated training data can often produce much the same effect as encoding them in the model architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the right way to frame it is that synthetic data is really the only lever we have, at the moment, for getting certain kinds of structure into a model that you can't get just by scaling up the natural data. When you train on text scraped from the web, you're getting whatever distribution of behaviors happens to be out there, and a lot of the things we actually want, like compositional generalization, or the ability to follow a particular format reliably, or being robust to some weird perturbation of the input, those just aren't well-represented in that distribution. You might get them for free at scale, or you might not, and you don't really get to choose.

So the way I think about synthetic data is as a way of writing down a constraint in a form the model can actually consume. If I have some belief about how the model ought to behave, say, "if these two premises are true, then this conclusion follows," or "the meaning of this sentence shouldn't change if I swap in a synonym," I can't inject that belief into the parameters directly. But I can turn it into a generative procedure, sample a bunch of examples that satisfy the constraint, and train on those. It's a slightly indirect way of specifying an inductive bias, but it's one that works with the training pipeline we already have rather than requiring you to redesign the architecture.

And a lot of the work in my group has been in that spirit. We did some early stuff on data augmentation for compositional generalization, where the idea was basically: if you see the fragment "jump twice" and you see "walk" and "walk twice," then you have evidence that "jump" and "walk" are substitutable, so you can synthesize "jump twice" examples even if they never appeared. That's a top-down constraint, it's a belief about substitutability, but it gets expressed entirely through the data. More recently we've been looking at things where you use a language model itself to generate the data, which lets you express much richer constraints, because now the "generative procedure" can be a natural language description of the behavior you want.

The thing I'd caution against, though, is thinking of synthetic data as free. Every time you generate it, you're baking in the assumptions of the generator, and if those assumptions are wrong, or too narrow, the model learns the wrong thing with great confidence. There's a real tension between the constraint being precise enough to be useful and the data being diverse enough that the model doesn't just memorize the template. So I tend to think of it less as "here's a trick for getting more data" and more as "here's a way of making your modeling assumptions explicit," and that means you should be able to say, in words, what the assumption is, and have some way of checking whether it's actually the right one.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data can express constraints through the existing training pipeline without redesigning the architecture. It does not claim this often works as well as encoding constraints in the architecture.

astra-6.text:
I think synthetic data gives us an interesting way to specify what we want a model to learn. Usually, we start with a big collection of naturally occurring text and hope that the patterns we care about are represented in it. With synthetic data, we can start with a hypothesis about a behavior we want and construct examples that make that behavior useful or necessary.

For example, if we want a model to use a particular piece of evidence, we can construct pairs of examples where we change that evidence and the correct answer changes with it. That gives us a way to communicate a constraint through the training distribution, even when it’s difficult to express that constraint directly in the architecture or the loss function.

The caveat is that a constraint on your data isn’t automatically a constraint on the model. There might be some shortcut in the examples you generated, and the model might learn that instead of the rule you had in mind. So I think the exciting possibility is to use synthetic data as a controlled intervention: articulate a principle, generate examples, and then test whether the resulting behavior generalizes beyond the particular way you constructed those examples.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data can communicate constraints through the training distribution, especially when direct architectural expression is difficult, but does not claim this often works as well as encoding constraints in the architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think synthetic data gives us a way to express the behavior we want in terms of examples, rather than trying to write down a constraint directly on the model’s parameters. If we want a model to respect some rule, we can generate situations where that rule matters and train on the appropriate behavior. That’s a fairly flexible interface for injecting top-down knowledge into learning.

The hard part is that the generator has to get the distinction right. If you use a model to generate the data, you can inherit its mistakes or create shortcuts that let the student succeed without learning the intended rule. So I’d want to separate generating examples from checking them wherever possible, and then evaluate on cases that weren’t produced by the same process.

There’s also a difference between encouraging a constraint and guaranteeing it. Synthetic data can make a behavior more likely, but training on examples generally doesn’t establish that the model will obey the rule in every new setting. I think it’s a useful tool for shaping behavior, especially when the constraint is easier to demonstrate than to formalize, but you still need to understand where that generalization breaks down.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic examples can shape behavior and are a flexible alternative to directly constraining model parameters. It does not state that this often works as well as encoding constraints in the model’s architecture.
